concordance.evidence_span: If the protocol proposes to use AI or other derivation methods, the protocol should specify the assumptions and parameters of the computer algorithms used, the data source from which the information was used to build the algorithm, whether the algorithm was supervised (i.e., using input and review by experts) or unsupervised, and the metrics associated with validation of the methods.
concordance.rationale: Asks that descriptions of source data, algorithm performance and training data be accepted in place of algorithm specifications; the final keeps the same specification list unchanged.
Asks the guidance to reference other HHS/FDA projects (e.g., FHIR-to-CDISC mapping); this concerns external initiatives rather than the guidance's own recommendations.

concordance.evidence_span: Data curation and transformation into a CDM, as well as general QA/QC procedures, are discussed in section VI, Data Quality During Data Accrual, Curation, and Transformation into the Final Study-Specific Dataset.
concordance.rationale: Asks for the expected level of documentation when harmonization relies on a CDM; the final adds no such detail beyond a cross-reference to section VI.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks for accepted standards and methods for demonstrating completeness; the final only rewords 'each data source' to 'proposed data source(s)' and adds no methods.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks for a definition and examples of 'key covariates'; the final sentence is unchanged on this point and no definition was added.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether details apply to the study population or the whole data source population; the final does not clarify this.

concordance.evidence_span: When using medical claims data sources, continuity of coverage should be addressed, given that patients often enroll and disenroll in different health plans when they experience changes in employment, or other life circumstances. When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks that enrollment/disenrollment be tied to claims (insurance enrollment) data; the final now addresses continuity of coverage specifically for claims and continuity of care for EHRs.

concordance.evidence_span: When using medical claims data sources, continuity of coverage should be addressed, given that patients often enroll and disenroll in different health plans when they experience changes in employment, or other life circumstances. When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks that continuity language be delineated separately for EHR and claims data; the final is concordant, splitting continuity of coverage (claims) from continuity of care (EHR).

concordance.evidence_span: The validity of findings from a study using these data depends in part on the documentation of the migration of patients into and out of health plans and health care systems. Such documentation allows for the identification of time periods during which data are and are not available on the patients of interest.
concordance.rationale: Asks for a term like 'continuity of observable period'; the final introduces 'continuity of care' and refers to time periods when data are and are not available, but not the proposed term.

concordance.evidence_span: Definitions of continuity of coverage and continuity of care should be developed and documented in the protocol. Of note, information on continuity of care may be difficult to accurately capture (e.g., data do not differentiate discontinuation of care and lack of encounters due to worsening or resolution of existing health conditions) and might need to be approximated in an EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks how to define eligibility/observation in EHRs lacking enrollment files; the final adds continuity-of-care definitions and notes it may need to be approximated, without detailed method.
Asks to distinguish closed from open claims sources; searched IV.B.1 and the whole final, no such distinction appears.

concordance.evidence_span: A second example is a study where an outcome is dependent on a specific frequency of laboratory tests, and clinicians do not typically order those tests at such a frequency.
concordance.rationale: Asks to replace the lab-test-frequency example with one about outcomes absent from claims; the example is retained unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: Information should be provided about the distribution of length of follow-up for patients in the data sources because the length of follow-up may inform whether the selected data sources are adequate or whether additional supportive data are needed to ascertain long latency outcomes.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether a feasibility assessment of follow-up across candidate sources is expected before selection; the final follow-up text is essentially unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: If these exposures are particularly relevant to the study question, the data source may not be suitable, or the protocol should describe how this information gap will be addressed (e.g., by building additional modules into the EHR system, linking, or collecting additional data).
concordance.rationale: Proposes an e.g. on addressing information gaps (adding EHR modules or collecting data outside the EHR); the final adds a closely matching parenthetical.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks that linkage rate and sample-size trade-offs be recognized as a feasibility factor; the final adds 'acceptable sample size' to the multi-source integration sentence but does not discuss linkage rate.
Asks whether unpublished vendor statements on linkage quality suffice; searched IV.B.2 and VI.A, the final does not address vendor-supplied linkage evidence.

concordance.evidence_span: De-identification of patient records and any process that could be used to re-identify unique patients in original source data without losing traceability (e.g., use of linkage tokens).
concordance.rationale: Asks the guidance to describe tokenization as a linkage method; the final only mentions 'linkage tokens' as an example in the de-identification item, not as a described linkage method.

concordance.evidence_span: Procedures for adjudicating discrepancies in linked data as well as plans for handling linkage discrepancies (e.g., adjusting risk estimates for the linkage error).
concordance.rationale: Asks for guidance on resolving value disagreements across linked sources; the corresponding VI.A item on adjudicating discrepancies is unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: Specific attention to data curation including individual level and population level linkages and understanding of many-to-one and 1:1 linkage is fundamental to assessing the appropriateness of a new data linkage.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether steps to obtain 1:1 linkage are expected; the final retains the same general sentence on many-to-one and 1:1 linkage.

concordance.evidence_span: Data linkages can be used to increase the amount of data available to capture the longitudinal patient journey, increase the amount of data available on individual patients, and provide additional data for validation purposes.
concordance.rationale: Asks to clarify 'breadth and depth of data'; the final replaces the phrase with explicit wording about the longitudinal patient journey and amount of data per patient.

concordance.evidence_span: FDA recommends considering and documenting the type of curation performed to address duplication or fragmentation issues and documenting approaches taken to address issues that cannot be fully rectified by curation.
concordance.rationale: Asks for specific recommendations on reconciling patients appearing in multiple sources; the final keeps the general curation-documentation recommendation without reconciliation methods.
Asks whether sponsors should routinely evaluate source data changes after a data cut; searched IV.B.2 and VI, no such recommendation was added.

concordance.evidence_span: If the study involves establishing new data linkages within the same data sources (e.g., mother-infant linkages) or across different data sources (e.g., vital records, disease and product registries, biobank data), the protocol should describe each data source, the information that will be obtained, linkage methods, and the accuracy and completeness of data linkages over time.
concordance.rationale: Proposes rewording 'internal/external data sources' to linkages within the same source or across different sources; the final adopts that framing.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks what 'acceptable quality' means or for an example; the final adds 'sample size' but does not define or illustrate acceptable quality.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks that heterogeneity documentation be limited to characteristics relevant to the hypothesis; the final drops 'population characteristics' from the heterogeneity list, a narrowing but not the relevance-based limit requested.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks for a rationale of when combining data sources is applicable; the final adds none.

concordance.evidence_span: Even where multiple data sources are linked by a unique patient identifier or where the patient information is coming from only one data source, there still can be an issue with multiple records or duplicate records.
concordance.rationale: Asks to replace the statement that duplicates are not an issue with a unique identifier, noting duplicates occur even within one source; the final makes exactly that change.

concordance.evidence_span: FDA recommends considering and documenting the type of curation performed to address duplication or fragmentation issues and documenting approaches taken to address issues that cannot be fully rectified by curation.
concordance.rationale: Asks for an example of curation to handle multiple records; the final sentence is unchanged and gives no example.

concordance.evidence_span: FDA recommends considering and documenting the type of curation performed to address duplication or fragmentation issues and documenting approaches taken to address issues that cannot be fully rectified by curation.
concordance.rationale: Asks that documentation may be provided jointly with third-party vendors; the final curation recommendation is unchanged and does not mention vendors.
Asks the section to reference FDA's separate Data Standards draft guidance; this concerns alignment with another guidance.
Asks FDA to state a preferred CDM for receiving RWD; searched IV.B.3 and the whole final, no preferred CDM is named.

concordance.evidence_span: Nevertheless, combining many data sources, especially with the addition of data transformation into a CDM, adds a layer of complexity that should be considered. Because there are many different configurations of distributed health data networks, the configurations discussed in this guidance should not be considered comprehensive.
concordance.rationale: Objects that the distributed data network material is excessive; the final retains the section with only editorial edits and adds a CDM definition.
Asks FDA to indicate acceptance of non-CDISC standards/CDMs (FHIR, OMOP); none are named in the final.

concordance.evidence_span: The computable phenotype definition, composed of standardized and mapped data elements and phenotype algorithm, if applicable, should be described in the protocol and study report and should also be available in a computer-processable format.
concordance.rationale: Asks to define 'computer-processable format' and whether code must be available; the final keeps the phrase undefined.
Asks whether model and training code should be made available; searched IV.B.4 and IV.B.5, the final does not address this.

concordance.evidence_span: Clinical validation of the computable phenotype definition should be described in the protocol and study report. For additional information on validation, see section IV.D, Validation: General Considerations.
concordance.rationale: Asks what should be described regarding clinical validation; the final sentence is unchanged apart from capitalization.

concordance.evidence_span: A computable phenotype identifies a clinical condition or characteristic using a computerized query to an EHR system or clinical data repository (including disease registries, claims data) using a defined set of data elements and logical expressions.
concordance.rationale: Asks to replace 'computable phenotype' with 'operational definition for the target patient population'; the final keeps the term and adds a glossary-derived definition instead.

concordance.evidence_span: Advances include natural language processing, machine learning, and particularly deep learning to: (1) extract data elements from unstructured text in EHRs; (2) develop computer algorithms that identify outcomes; or (3) evaluate images or laboratory results. FDA does not endorse any specific AI technology.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether FDA would consider AI-extracted endpoints from text; the final text on AI uses (including identifying outcomes) is substantively unchanged and adds no explicit statement.

concordance.evidence_span: Relevant impacts on data quality from use of AI or other computerized extraction methods should be documented in the protocol and analysis plan.
concordance.rationale: Proposes specifying that data-quality impacts are those from use of AI or other methods; the final adds 'from use of AI or other computerized extraction methods'.

concordance.evidence_span: If the protocol proposes to use AI or other derivation methods, the protocol should specify the assumptions and parameters of the computer algorithms used, the data source from which the information was used to build the algorithm, whether the algorithm was supervised (i.e., using input and review by experts) or unsupervised, and the metrics associated with validation of the methods.
concordance.rationale: Asks to allow algorithm details in an appendix or via publications; the final specification sentence is unchanged with no such allowance.

concordance.evidence_span: Relevant impacts on data quality from use of AI or other computerized extraction methods should be documented in the protocol and analysis plan.
concordance.rationale: Asks to clarify the requirement concerns AI/extraction methods rather than human abstraction; the final ties data-quality documentation to AI or other computerized extraction methods.
Asks that algorithm performance in relevant subgroups be reported to detect measurement bias; searched IV.B.5 and validation sections, no subgroup performance requirement was added.

concordance.evidence_span: The capture of patients’ health care information in a medical claim or EHR data source depends on continuity of coverage (i.e., enrollment and disenrollment from the health insurance plan) and continuity of care (i.e., continuous interaction with the health care system).
concordance.rationale: Asks to clarify that coverage includes both medical and drug coverage; the final defines continuity of coverage as plan enrollment/disenrollment without distinguishing drug coverage.

concordance.evidence_span: When using medical claims data sources, continuity of coverage should be addressed, given that patients often enroll and disenroll in different health plans when they experience changes in employment, or other life circumstances. When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks to use 'continuity of care' for EHRs; the final introduces continuity of care for EHR data sources alongside continuity of coverage for claims.

concordance.evidence_span: When using medical claims data sources, continuity of coverage should be addressed, given that patients often enroll and disenroll in different health plans when they experience changes in employment, or other life circumstances. When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks recommendations to be distinguished by data source type throughout; the final does so for continuity in IV.B.1 but not more broadly.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks for metrics indicating 'acceptable quality'; the final adds no metrics.

concordance.evidence_span: If the protocol proposes to use AI or other derivation methods, the protocol should specify the assumptions and parameters of the computer algorithms used, the data source from which the information was used to build the algorithm, whether the algorithm was supervised (i.e., using input and review by experts) or unsupervised, and the metrics associated with validation of the methods.
concordance.rationale: Asks for flexibility because sharing AI/ML algorithms and parameters may compromise IP; the final specification requirement is unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks for accepted standards for demonstrating completeness; the final adds none.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks for a definition and examples of 'key covariates'; none was added.

concordance.evidence_span: If these exposures are particularly relevant to the study question, the data source may not be suitable, or the protocol should describe how this information gap will be addressed (e.g., by building additional modules into the EHR system, linking, or collecting additional data).
concordance.rationale: Asks for text on how information gaps may be addressed (e.g., additional EHR modules); the final adds that example along with linking and additional data collection.

concordance.evidence_span: Data linkages can be used to increase the amount of data available to capture the longitudinal patient journey, increase the amount of data available on individual patients, and provide additional data for validation purposes.
concordance.rationale: Asks to clarify 'breadth and depth' as the longitudinal patient journey; the final uses that wording.

concordance.evidence_span: FDA recommends considering and documenting the type of curation performed to address duplication or fragmentation issues and documenting approaches taken to address issues that cannot be fully rectified by curation.
concordance.rationale: Asks for an example of issues not rectifiable by curation; the final sentence is unchanged with no example.

concordance.evidence_span: Differences in terminology and coding systems used in different health care systems should also be considered.
concordance.rationale: Asks that pooling across sources consider data element definitions and harmonization; the final adds in IV.A that terminology and coding differences across systems should be considered, but IV.B.3 is unchanged on harmonization.

concordance.evidence_span: The computable phenotype definition, composed of standardized and mapped data elements and phenotype algorithm, if applicable, should be described in the protocol and study report and should also be available in a computer-processable format.
concordance.rationale: Asks what 'computer-processable format' means; the final leaves it undefined.
Proposes establishing neutral data linkage brokers, an infrastructure matter outside the guidance text.

concordance.evidence_span: If the protocol proposes to use AI or other derivation methods, the protocol should specify the assumptions and parameters of the computer algorithms used, the data source from which the information was used to build the algorithm, whether the algorithm was supervised (i.e., using input and review by experts) or unsupervised, and the metrics associated with validation of the methods.
concordance.rationale: Asks FDA to reconsider algorithm disclosure given proprietary IP; the final specification requirement is unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: Obtaining comprehensive drug coverage and medical care data on patients with certain types of privacy concerns (e.g., sexually transmitted infection, substance abuse, mental health conditions) can be challenging and failure to do so can result in incomplete or erroneous information.
concordance.rationale: Asks to expand the privacy-concern list to vulnerable participants (children, adolescents, caregivers); the list is unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: When a probabilistic approach is used, the analysis plan should include testing the impact of the degree of match and robustness of findings.
concordance.rationale: Objects to requiring testing of degree of match for probabilistic linkage; the sentence is retained verbatim.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Proposes defining acceptable quality as no significant impact on data accuracy; the final does not adopt that wording.

concordance.evidence_span: A computable phenotype definition should include metadata and supporting information about the definition, its intended use, the clinical rationale or research justification for the definition, and data assessing validation in various health care settings (Richesson et al. 2016).
concordance.rationale: Asks for minimum metadata expectations (version, author, identifier, etc.); the metadata sentence is unchanged.
Asks for discussion of the disproportionate effect of coverage discontinuity on underserved populations; searched IV.B.1 and IV.A, no such discussion was added.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks for guidance distinguishing single versus multiple EHR system scenarios and how analyses across systems should be shown; the final adds no such analysis guidance.

concordance.evidence_span: In general, EHRs and medical claims data may not systematically capture the use of nonprescription drugs or drugs that are not reimbursed under health plans, episodes of medical tourism outside the U.S., or immunizations offered in the workplace, at pharmacies or public health clinics, or through government immunization programs.
concordance.rationale: Asks how acceptable OTC/non-reimbursed exposure data are if validated by a clinician in the EHR; the final softens 'do not' to 'may not' but gives no acceptability guidance.
Asks FDA to collaborate with ONC on FHIR; concerns FDA activity, not guidance text.
Asks FDA to collaborate with HL7 FHIR Accelerator projects; concerns FDA activity, not guidance text.
Asks sponsors to provide data enabling third-party validation through a CDM network such as Sentinel; no such recommendation appears in the final.

concordance.evidence_span: The computable phenotype definition, composed of standardized and mapped data elements and phenotype algorithm, if applicable, should be described in the protocol and study report and should also be available in a computer-processable format.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether source-database code suffices or emerging standards (e.g., CQL) should be used; the final adds 'standardized and mapped' data elements but does not address representation standards.
Asks FDA to acknowledge the lack of consistent phenotype representation methods and suggest a roadmap; the final contains no such acknowledgement.

concordance.evidence_span: In addition, medical claims data can change during the run-off period and claims adjudication process, as initial submissions may be adjusted or corrected, leading to variations in reported diagnoses and procedures over time.
concordance.rationale: Asks the guidance to note the need to check whether claims are final-adjudicated or unadjudicated; the final adds in section IV that claims can change during run-off and adjudication, without requiring sponsors to determine claim status.

concordance.evidence_span: When using medical claims data sources, continuity of coverage should be addressed, given that patients often enroll and disenroll in different health plans when they experience changes in employment, or other life circumstances. When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks to discuss enrollment for claims and observability for EHRs rather than coverage for EHRs; the final separates continuity of coverage (claims) from continuity of care (EHR).

concordance.evidence_span: A description of any available information on prescribing and utilization practices (e.g., stepped therapy, prior authorizations, formulary restrictions) that may impact feasibility of the study in the data source or interpretation of study findings.
concordance.rationale: Asks that formulary be considered when discussing drug exposure availability; the final adds formulary restrictions to the IV.A list of prescribing practices affecting feasibility, not in IV.B.1.

concordance.evidence_span: The probabilistic approach for data linkage uses less restrictive steps in which the linkage can be established by exact matching of fewer identifiers or matching part of the information on the identifiers (e.g., the first several letters of a name) (Carreras et al., 2018).
concordance.rationale: Asks the section to refer readers to published linkage recommendations; the final keeps the same single citation and adds no further references.

concordance.evidence_span: Quality of record linkage (i.e., linking records from multiple datasets) and deduplication (i.e., finding duplicate records in a dataset) process, which may vary depending on the accuracy of the data used to perform the matches and the accuracy of the linkage algorithm.
concordance.rationale: Asks for direction on assessing linkage quality; the related VI.A items on linkage quality and errors are essentially unchanged.

concordance.evidence_span: Nevertheless, combining many data sources, especially with the addition of data transformation into a CDM, adds a layer of complexity that should be considered. Because there are many different configurations of distributed health data networks, the configurations discussed in this guidance should not be considered comprehensive.
concordance.rationale: Asks for mention of site-specific variation in data quality across network sites; the final adds no such text.

concordance.evidence_span: A computable phenotype definition should include metadata and supporting information about the definition, its intended use, the clinical rationale or research justification for the definition, and data assessing validation in various health care settings (Richesson et al. 2016).
concordance.rationale: Asks which data elements are requested and whether requirements extend to other algorithms; the final does not clarify this.

concordance.evidence_span: A computable phenotype identifies a clinical condition or characteristic using a computerized query to an EHR system or clinical data repository (including disease registries, claims data) using a defined set of data elements and logical expressions.
concordance.rationale: Asks for specific recommendations on computable phenotypes; the final adds a definition and 'standardized and mapped data elements' but little further specific guidance.

concordance.evidence_span: Although medical claims data are typically in structured fields, large amounts of key clinical data are unstructured data within EHRs, either as free text data fields (such as physician notes) or as other non-standardized information in computer documents (such as PDF-based radiology reports).
concordance.rationale: Asks to make explicit that the unstructured-data section is not relevant to claims; the final opens by noting claims data are typically structured.

concordance.evidence_span: All these methods are computer-assisted to various levels but require a significant amount of human-aided curation and decision-making, injecting an additional level of data variability and quality considerations into the final study-specific dataset.
concordance.rationale: Asks for additional cautionary language on unstructured EHR data; the final adds no new cautions beyond dropping 'currently'.

concordance.evidence_span: AI is a branch of computer science, statistics, and engineering that uses algorithms or models to perform tasks and exhibit behaviors such as learning, making decisions, and making predictions.
concordance.rationale: Objects to mentioning AI in this context; the final retains the AI discussion and adds an in-text AI definition.
Asks FDA to issue a future dedicated AI guidance; concerns other guidances.
Proposes creating an open-source linkage algorithm to replace proprietary vendor algorithms; this is an infrastructure proposal outside the guidance text.

concordance.evidence_span: De-identification of patient records and any process that could be used to re-identify unique patients in original source data without losing traceability (e.g., use of linkage tokens).
concordance.rationale: Asks what detailed information is required for linkage/tokenization methods; the final only mentions linkage tokens as an example and specifies no disclosure requirements.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks to clarify 'demonstrating' and limit it to study-critical elements; the final keeps 'demonstrating' without such clarification.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks to change 'demonstrate' to 'describe and justify'; the final keeps 'demonstrate'.

concordance.evidence_span: The computable phenotype definition, composed of standardized and mapped data elements and phenotype algorithm, if applicable, should be described in the protocol and study report and should also be available in a computer-processable format.
concordance.rationale: Proposes inserting 'standardized and mapped' data elements and 'if applicable'; the final adopts this wording.

concordance.evidence_span: If the operational definition includes information abstracted from unstructured data in the EHRs or another data source (e.g., mention of spina bifida in birth certificate records for the identification of neural tube defects in infants), the protocol should provide a detailed description and rationale for the methods and tools used to process the unstructured data and the validation of those methods.
concordance.rationale: Asks whether the extraction process for unstructured data should be justified for quality and validity when used for outcomes; the corresponding V.D.2 text is unchanged and no new clarification was added.

concordance.evidence_span: When using EHR data sources, continuity of care should be discussed, specifically, whether patients receive all types of health care services within the same health system or network of facilities that contribute to the same EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks for expectations on coverage captured in EHR data; the final adds a continuity-of-care discussion specific to EHR data sources.
Asks for measures to mitigate AI bias that amplifies inequities; searched IV.B.5 and elsewhere, no such content added.

concordance.evidence_span: For studies that require combining data from multiple data sources or study sites, FDA recommends demonstrating whether and how data from different sources can be obtained and integrated with acceptable sample size and quality, given the potential for heterogeneity in clinical and coding practices across data sources or systems.
concordance.rationale: Asks that patient attrition from low linkage rates be considered; the final adds 'acceptable sample size' to the integration sentence, partially reflecting this.
Asks to note increased re-identification risk from linking datasets; searched IV.B.2 and VI.A, no such statement was added.

concordance.evidence_span: Sponsors should demonstrate that the proposed data source(s) contain the detail and completeness needed to capture the study populations, exposures, key covariates, outcomes of interest, and other important parameters (e.g., time periods) that are relevant to the study question and design.
concordance.rationale: Asks for publications on accepted completeness standards; none were added.

concordance.evidence_span: The capture of patients’ health care information in a medical claim or EHR data source depends on continuity of coverage (i.e., enrollment and disenrollment from the health insurance plan) and continuity of care (i.e., continuous interaction with the health care system).
concordance.rationale: Asks for distinct terms for time in a health system versus insurance coverage; the final introduces 'continuity of care' alongside 'continuity of coverage'.

concordance.evidence_span: Definitions of continuity of coverage and continuity of care should be developed and documented in the protocol. Of note, information on continuity of care may be difficult to accurately capture (e.g., data do not differentiate discontinuation of care and lack of encounters due to worsening or resolution of existing health conditions) and might need to be approximated in an EHR data source.
concordance.rationale: Asks to acknowledge proxy measures of continuity when enrollment records are absent; the final states continuity of care might need to be approximated in an EHR data source.

concordance.evidence_span: The validity of findings from a study using these data depends in part on the documentation of the migration of patients into and out of health plans and health care systems. Such documentation allows for the identification of time periods during which data are and are not available on the patients of interest.
concordance.rationale: Asks to incorporate observability and focus less on continuity; the final refers to time periods when data are or are not available but retains and expands the continuity framing.

concordance.evidence_span: Probabilistic and deterministic approaches to data linkage may result in different linkage quality, albeit both approaches can have value depending on the scenario.
concordance.rationale: Asks to underscore well-executed methodology as the key linkage principle; the final sentence on linkage approaches is unchanged.
